sources.title: Dose-response relationship between weekly resistance training volume and increases in muscle mass: A systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.authors: Schoenfeld BJ, Ogborn D, Krieger JW
sources.summaryEn: Systematic review and meta-regression of 34 treatment groups from 15 studies examining total weekly resistance-training sets and muscle-size changes. Each additional weekly set was associated with a small increase in hypertrophy effect size (P=0.002), and higher- vs lower-volume categories differed significantly (P=0.03), but a three-level categorical model (<5, 5-9, 10+ sets) showed only a non-significant trend (P=0.074). The authors describe a graded dose-response relationship, while noting the modest number of included studies and indirect volume manipulation across trials.

sources.title: The Resistance Training Dose Response: Meta-Regressions Exploring the Effects of Weekly Volume and Frequency on Muscle Hypertrophy and Strength Gains
sources.authors: Pelland JC, Remmert JF, Robinson ZP, Hinson SR, Zourdos MC
sources.summaryEn: Series of multilevel meta-regressions across 67 studies (2058 participants) that classify contributing sets as 'direct', 'fractional', or 'total' relative to the measured muscle/lift before modeling dose-response curves for weekly volume and frequency. Using the best-supported 'fractional' method, both hypertrophy and strength increased with volume (100% posterior probability of a positive slope) but with diminishing returns, more pronounced for strength; frequency showed a negligible-compatible effect on hypertrophy but a positive, diminishing-returns effect on strength. Authors emphasize the distinction between direct and indirect sets as central to interpretation and flag that dose-response curves are not linear.

sources.title: A Systematic Review of The Effects of Different Resistance Training Volumes on Muscle Hypertrophy
sources.authors: Baz-Valle E, Balsalobre-Fernández C, Alix-Fages C, Santos-Concejero J
sources.summaryEn: Systematic review/meta-analysis of 7 RCTs (6 in the quantitative synthesis) in young trained men (18-35y, ≥1y experience) comparing low (<12), moderate (12-20), and high (>20) weekly sets per muscle on muscle thickness/CSA. No significant difference was found between moderate and high volume for quadriceps (p=0.19) or biceps brachii (p=0.59), while high volume showed an advantage for triceps brachii (p=0.01); authors suggest 12-20 weekly sets as a practical standard. The evidence base is small (6-7 studies) and restricted to young trained men, limiting generalizability.

sources.title: Effects of Resistance Training Frequency on Measures of Muscle Hypertrophy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
sources.authors: Schoenfeld BJ, Ogborn D, Krieger JW
sources.summaryEn: Systematic review/meta-analysis of 10 studies comparing weekly resistance-training frequencies for muscle hypertrophy. Higher frequency was associated with a significantly greater hypertrophy effect size than lower frequency overall (0.49 vs 0.30, P=0.002); among volume-equated studies, training a muscle group twice weekly outperformed once weekly, but whether 3x/week is superior to 2x/week could not be reliably estimated due to inadequate sample size for that comparison.

sources.title: How many times per week should a muscle be trained to maximize muscle hypertrophy? A systematic review and meta-analysis of studies examining the effects of resistance training frequency
sources.authors: Schoenfeld BJ, Grgic J, Krieger J
sources.summaryEn: Systematic review/meta-analysis of 25 studies on weekly training frequency and muscle hypertrophy. On a volume-equated basis, no significant differences were found between frequencies across direct-growth-measure studies, resistance-trained individuals, or upper/lower body; a meta-regression restricted to non-volume-equated studies favored higher frequency, but the magnitude of difference between 1x and 3+x/week was modest. Authors conclude frequency does not meaningfully affect hypertrophy once weekly volume is held constant.

sources.title: Effect of Resistance Training Frequency on Gains in Muscular Strength: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
sources.authors: Grgic J, Schoenfeld BJ, Davies TB, Lazinica B, Krieger JW, Pedisic Z
sources.summaryEn: Systematic review/meta-analysis of 22 studies on resistance-training frequency and muscular strength gains. Overall effect sizes rose with frequency (1, 2, 3, 4+ times/week; p=0.003), but this effect disappeared in the volume-equated subgroup (p=0.421), indicating the raw frequency effect is largely attributable to accompanying differences in training volume rather than frequency itself. Subgroup effects varied by exercise type (multi- vs single-joint), body region, age, and sex, and most included studies used untrained participants.

sources.title: Influence of Resistance Training Proximity-to-Failure on Skeletal Muscle Hypertrophy: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis
sources.authors: Refalo MC, Helms ER, Trexler ET, Hamilton DL, Fyfe JJ
sources.summaryEn: Systematic review/meta-analysis of 15 studies comparing resistance training to momentary muscular failure vs non-failure, 'set failure' (any definition) vs non-failure, or different velocity-loss thresholds, for muscle hypertrophy. A small, borderline-significant advantage was found for training to any definition of set failure over non-failure (ES=0.19, p=0.045), but no significant advantage emerged specifically for momentary muscular failure vs non-failure (ES=0.12, p=0.343), nor for high (>25%) vs moderate (20-25%) velocity-loss thresholds (ES=0.08, p=0.529) — suggesting a potentially non-linear relationship between proximity-to-failure and hypertrophy rather than a simple 'closer is always better' pattern.

sources.title: Exploring the Dose-Response Relationship Between Estimated Resistance Training Proximity to Failure, Strength Gain, and Muscle Hypertrophy: A Series of Meta-Regressions
sources.authors: Robinson ZP, Pelland JC, Remmert JF, Refalo MC, Jukic I, Steele J, Zourdos MC
sources.summaryEn: Exploratory multilevel meta-regression series estimating repetitions-in-reserve (RIR) at set termination (estimated from training-intervention descriptions, a stated limitation) and its association with strength and hypertrophy, adjusting for load, volume-equating method, duration, and training status. In all best-fit models for strength, RIR's marginal slope confidence intervals contained zero (negligible relationship); for hypertrophy, slopes were consistently negative with CIs excluding zero, indicating greater hypertrophy as sets were taken closer to failure while strength gains were similar across a wide RIR range. The authors explicitly describe the models as exploratory with only modest overall fit and caution that exact RIR-outcome relationships remain unclear given the estimation procedure.

sources.title: Effects of resistance training performed to repetition failure or non-failure on muscular strength and hypertrophy: A systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.authors: Grgic J, Schoenfeld BJ, Orazem J, Sabol F
sources.journal: Journal of Sport and Health Science
sources.summaryEn: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 15 studies (all young-adult participants) comparing resistance training to repetition failure vs. non-failure on muscular strength and hypertrophy, with subgroup analyses by training status, volume equating, body region, exercise selection, and study design. No significant overall difference was found for strength (ES=-0.09, 95%CI -0.22 to 0.05) or hypertrophy (ES=0.22, 95%CI -0.11 to 0.55); in studies that did not equate training volume between groups, non-failure training significantly favored strength gains (ES=-0.32, 95%CI -0.57 to -0.07), while in the subgroup of resistance-trained individuals, training to failure showed a small but significant hypertrophy advantage (ES=0.15, 95%CI 0.03-0.26). The authors conclude training to failure is not required for strength or hypertrophy gains but does not appear detrimental, and call for more research in older adults and highly trained populations.

sources.title: Effects of Resistance Training Performed to Failure or Not to Failure on Muscle Strength, Hypertrophy, and Power Output: A Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis
sources.authors: Vieira AF, Umpierre D, Teodoro JL, Lisboa SC, Baroni BM, Izquierdo M, Cadore EL
sources.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
sources.summaryEn: Systematic review/meta-analysis of 13 studies (≥6-week RT interventions) comparing training to failure (RTF) vs not to failure (RTNF) on strength, hypertrophy, and power. No difference was found for maximal strength overall (SMD=-0.08, p=0.642), but RTNF showed greater strength gains under non-equalized volumes (SMD=-0.34, p=0.048); RTF showed greater hypertrophy overall (SMD=0.75, p=0.005), yet this advantage disappeared once volume was equalized between conditions; RTNF also showed better power outcomes under non-equalized volumes (SMD=-0.61, p=0.025), with no overall power difference (SMD=-0.20, p=0.239). Authors conclude non-failure training can match or exceed failure training for strength/power while hypertrophy differences depend on whether volume is equated.

sources.title: Novel Resistance Training-Specific Rating of Perceived Exertion Scale Measuring Repetitions in Reserve
sources.authors: Zourdos MC, Klemp A, Dolan C, Quiles JM, Schau KA, Jo E, Helms E, Esgro B, Duncan S, Garcia Merino S, Blanco R
sources.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
sources.summaryEn: Cross-sectional validity study (n=29: 15 experienced, 14 novice squatters) testing whether a repetitions-in-reserve (RIR) based RPE scale tracks bar velocity during a 1RM squat test and an 8-rep set at 70% 1RM. Strong inverse correlations between average velocity and RPE were found in both experienced (r=-0.88) and novice (r=-0.77) lifters, and experienced lifters reported higher RPE at 1RM than novices despite similar velocities at submaximal loads. This supports RIR-based RPE as a practical, velocity-correlated intensity-monitoring tool, but the study is a single acute cross-sectional comparison, not a longitudinal training trial, so it speaks to concurrent/construct validity rather than training outcomes.

sources.title: Application of the Repetitions in Reserve-Based Rating of Perceived Exertion Scale for Resistance Training
sources.authors: Helms ER, Cronin J, Storey A, Zourdos MC
sources.summaryEn: Applied/narrative article (not a primary data study) explaining how to implement the repetitions-in-reserve (RIR) based RPE scale to autoregulate resistance-training loads on a set-by-set basis, arguing it can more precisely gauge near-limit intensity than session-level RPE and adjust loads to daily athlete capability. As a practical-application piece it synthesizes prior validity work (e.g., Zourdos et al. 2016) into coaching guidance rather than presenting new empirical findings.

sources.title: Effect of Training Leading to Repetition Failure on Muscular Strength: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
sources.authors: Davies T, Orr R, Halaki M, Hackett D
sources.summaryEn: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 8 studies comparing repetition-failure vs non-failure resistance training for muscular strength. A small pooled effect favored non-failure training (ES=0.34, p=0.02, corresponding to a 0.6-1.3% greater strength increase), with significant subgroup effects for compound exercises and trained participants, and a larger effect when training volume was not equated between conditions; no significant effect emerged in the volume-controlled subgroup. Authors conclude the small benefit of non-failure training is unlikely to be practically meaningful, so failure training is not necessary to maximize strength and, if used, should be applied sparingly given injury/overtraining risk. An erratum (Sports Med. 2016;46(4):605-610, doi:10.1007/s40279-016-0509-x, PMID 26893097) corrected calculation errors in the original analysis; this summary reflects the corrected/current PubMed record.

sources.title: Effects of velocity loss during resistance training on athletic performance, strength gains and muscle adaptations
sources.authors: Pareja-Blanco F, Rodríguez-Rosell D, Sánchez-Medina L, Sanchis-Moysi J, Dorado C, Mora-Custodio R, Yáñez-García JM, Morales-Alamo D, Pérez-Suárez I, Calbet JAL, González-Badillo JJ
sources.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports
sources.summaryEn: Randomized controlled trial (n=22 young men, 12 in VL20 and 10 in VL40, 8-week squat-only program) comparing a 20% (VL20) vs 40% (VL40) within-set velocity-loss threshold, assessed via MRI, muscle biopsy (fiber CSA/type), 1RM/load-velocity profile, countermovement jump, and 20-m sprint. VL20 produced similar squat strength gains to VL40 despite performing 40% fewer repetitions, and greater CMJ improvement (9.5% vs 3.5%, P<0.05), whereas VL40 produced greater hypertrophy of vastus lateralis/intermedius and a reduction in type IIX fiber percentage (preserved under VL20). Authors conclude that greater within-set fatigue/velocity loss meaningfully shapes both functional and structural adaptations, though the study is limited by small sample size (n=22), single-exercise (squat) design, and short (8-week) duration.

sources.title: Evidence-Based Guidelines for Resistance Training Volume to Maximize Muscle Hypertrophy
sources.authors: Schoenfeld B, Grgic J
sources.summaryEn: Narrative practical-application article (not indexed in PubMed) that translates the resistance-training-volume dose-response literature into evidence-based programming guidance specifically for maximizing muscle hypertrophy. Per its Crossref-listed abstract, the article 'provides evidence-based guidelines as to volume when creating RT programs designed to maximize muscle hypertrophy'; it synthesizes prior meta-analytic findings (e.g., Schoenfeld et al. 2017) into applied recommendations rather than reporting new primary data or a new meta-analysis.

sources.title: American College of Sports Medicine position stand. Progression models in resistance training for healthy adults
sources.authors: American College of Sports Medicine
sources.summaryEn: ACSM position stand giving expert-consensus, evidence-informed recommendations for progressive resistance training program design by training status (novice/intermediate/advanced) and goal (strength, hypertrophy, power, local muscular endurance) — e.g., 8-12RM loading and 2-3 days/week for novices; periodized 1-12RM emphasizing 6-12RM with higher-volume multi-set programs for hypertrophy; frequency scaling from 2-3 (novice) to 3-4 (intermediate) to 4-5 (advanced) days/week with training experience. As a position stand it aggregates the RCT and observational evidence available at the time plus expert judgment rather than presenting a new meta-analysis, and several of its specific quantitative recommendations (e.g., precise volume dose-response, frequency effects) have since been refined by more recent meta-analyses and meta-regressions.

sources.title: Does Training to Failure Maximize Muscle Hypertrophy?
sources.authors: Schoenfeld BJ, Grgic J
sources.summaryEn: Narrative practical-application article (not indexed in PubMed) examining whether training to muscular failure is a necessary strategy to maximize hypertrophy. Per its Crossref-listed abstract, the article 'examines the research behind these claims and attempts to draw evidence-based conclusions as to the practical implications for hypertrophy training'; it reviews and interprets existing proximity-to-failure research (including meta-analyses such as Davies et al. 2016 and related work) rather than presenting new primary data.

sources.title: Strength and Hypertrophy Adaptations Between Low- vs. High-Load Resistance Training: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
sources.authors: Schoenfeld BJ, Grgic J, Ogborn D, Krieger JW
sources.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
sources.summaryEn: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 21 studies comparing low-load (≤60% 1RM) versus high-load (>60% 1RM) resistance training performed to muscular failure. Found significantly greater dynamic 1RM strength gains with high-load training, while hypertrophy gains were statistically similar across load ranges. Restricted to failure-based protocols of ≥6 weeks in healthy, uninjured participants, so findings may not generalize to non-failure training.

sources.title: Resistance Training Load Effects on Muscle Hypertrophy and Strength Gain: Systematic Review and Network Meta-analysis
sources.authors: Lopez P, Radaelli R, Taaffe DR, Newton RU, Galvão DA, Trajano GS, Teodoro JL, Kraemer WJ, Häkkinen K, Pinto RS
sources.summaryEn: Network meta-analysis of 28 studies (747 healthy adults) comparing low (>15RM), moderate (9-15RM), and high (≤8RM) load resistance training performed to volitional failure. Hypertrophy gains were statistically similar across loads overall, though untrained participants showed greater hypertrophy and more-trained participants benefited from higher session frequency; strength gains were significantly greater with moderate and high loads than low loads. Restricted to failure-based training, limiting generalizability to non-failure protocols. Has a published erratum/corrigendum (Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2022 Feb 1;54(2):370, doi: 10.1249/MSS.0000000000002838, PMID 35029596).

sources.title: Effects of different intensities of resistance training with equated volume load on muscle strength and hypertrophy
sources.authors: Lasevicius T, Ugrinowitsch C, Schoenfeld BJ, Roschel H, Tavares LD, De Souza EO, Laurentino G, Tricoli V
sources.summaryEn: Within-subject randomized trial in 30 men comparing elbow-flexion and leg-press training at 20%, 40%, 60%, and 80% 1RM, with one limb trained at 20% 1RM and the contralateral limb randomized to 40%, 60%, or 80%, volume matched across intensities, for 12 weeks. All intensities increased 1RM strength and muscle cross-sectional area (CSA) over time, but 20% 1RM was suboptimal, and only 80% 1RM produced significantly greater CSA than 20% 1RM at 12 weeks, with strength gain magnitude also higher in the 60% and 80% groups. The small sample and within-subject, contralateral-limb design may limit generalization to conventional bilateral training programs.

sources.title: Muscle hypertrophy and strength gains after resistance training with different volume-matched loads: a systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.authors: Carvalho L, Junior RM, Barreira J, Schoenfeld BJ, Orazem J, Barroso R
sources.summaryEn: Systematic review and meta-analysis comparing muscle hypertrophy and strength gains across very-low, low, moderate, and high relative-load resistance training protocols with volume load (sets×reps×weight) equated between conditions. Higher loads produced significantly greater 1RM strength gains than lower loads even when volume load was matched, while hypertrophy outcomes were statistically similar regardless of load magnitude. Restricted to studies with volume-load matching, so it does not address unmatched or maximal-effort training designs.

sources.title: Longer Interset Rest Periods Enhance Muscle Strength and Hypertrophy in Resistance-Trained Men
sources.authors: Schoenfeld BJ, Pope ZK, Benik FM, Hester GM, Sellers J, Nooner JL, Schnaiter JA, Bond-Williams KE, Carter AS, Ross CL, Just BL, Henselmans M, Krieger JW
sources.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
sources.summaryEn: RCT in 21 resistance-trained men comparing 1-minute versus 3-minute inter-set rest intervals over an 8-week whole-body program with all other variables held constant. Longer rest intervals produced significantly greater gains in 1RM squat and bench press and greater anterior-thigh muscle thickness, with no group difference in muscular endurance. Small sample of young trained men limits generalizability to other populations or single-joint/isolation protocols.

sources.title: Effects of Rest Interval Duration in Resistance Training on Measures of Muscular Strength: A Systematic Review
sources.authors: Grgic J, Schoenfeld BJ, Skrepnik M, Davies TB, Mikulic P
sources.summaryEn: PRISMA-guided systematic review of 23 studies (491 participants: 413 males, 78 females) evaluating chronic muscular-strength adaptations to different inter-set rest-interval durations, with methodological quality (via a modified Downs and Black checklist) rated good-to-moderate across all included studies (none poor). Concluded that longer rest intervals (>2 minutes) appear needed to maximize strength gains in resistance-trained individuals, while short-to-moderate intervals (60-120s) may suffice for untrained individuals, though robust strength gains occurred even with rest intervals <60s. Findings are a narrative synthesis of individual studies rather than a pooled statistical meta-analysis.

sources.title: Volume Load Rather Than Resting Interval Influences Muscle Hypertrophy During High-Intensity Resistance Training
sources.authors: Longo AR, Silva-Batista C, Pedroso K, de Salles Painelli V, Lasevicius T, Schoenfeld BJ, Aihara AY, de Almeida Peres B, Tricoli V, Teixeira EL
sources.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
sources.summaryEn: Controlled trial in 28 participants using unilateral knee-extension protocols (each leg randomized to one of four rest-interval/volume-load combinations) comparing long (3-min) versus short (1-min) rest intervals, with and without volume-load matching, over 10 weeks at 80% 1RM. All protocols increased 1RM similarly (26.5-31.2%), but quadriceps cross-sectional area increased significantly more in protocols with higher volume load (LI: 13.1%, VLI-SI: 12.9%) than in lower volume-load protocols (SI: 6.8%, VSI-LI: 6.6%), regardless of rest interval, indicating volume load rather than rest interval per se drives the hypertrophic difference. Single-joint, single-exercise design in a modest sample limits broader generalization.

sources.title: Give it a rest: a systematic review with Bayesian meta-analysis on the effect of inter-set rest interval duration on muscle hypertrophy
sources.authors: Singer A, Wolf M, Generoso L, Arias E, Delcastillo K, Echevarria E, Martinez A, Androulakis Korakakis P, Refalo MC, Swinton PA, Schoenfeld BJ
sources.journal: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
sources.summaryEn: Pre-registered (OSF) systematic review with Bayesian meta-analysis of 19 measurements from 9 randomized studies comparing inter-set rest-interval durations for muscle hypertrophy. Central estimates modestly favored rest intervals over ~60 seconds for the arm and thigh, but showed little added benefit beyond roughly 90 seconds, with substantial heterogeneity, wide credible intervals, and results unaffected by whether sets were taken to failure. Authors describe the effect as a small, uncertain hypertrophic benefit rather than a strong or precisely estimated one.

sources.title: The Influence of Movement Tempo During Resistance Training on Muscular Strength and Hypertrophy Responses: A Review
sources.authors: Wilk M, Zajac A, Tufano JJ
sources.summaryEn: Narrative review examining how movement tempo (concentric and eccentric phase duration) influences chronic resistance-training adaptations. Concludes that available evidence on tempo manipulation is inconsistent/inconclusive, that most hypertrophy guidelines implicitly reflect self-selected ('volitional') tempos, and that no study has isolated the impact of eccentric-versus-concentric phase duration on chronic adaptations, offering qualitative practical recommendations instead. As a narrative synthesis (not a systematic review or meta-analysis), conclusions reflect the authors' interpretation rather than pooled quantitative evidence.

sources.title: Progressive overload without progressing load? The effects of load or repetition progression on muscular adaptations
sources.authors: Plotkin D, Coleman M, Van Every D, Maldonado J, Oberlin D, Israetel M, Feather J, Alto A, Vigotsky AD, Schoenfeld BJ
sources.summaryEn: RCT in 43 resistance-trained individuals comparing 8 weeks of lower-body training progressed either by increasing load at constant repetitions or by increasing repetitions at constant load. Rectus femoris hypertrophy modestly favored the repetitions-progression group while dynamic strength gains slightly favored the load-progression group, though most other between-group differences (other muscle sites, endurance, jump height, body composition) were small with confidence intervals crossing zero. Short 8-week duration and modest subgroup sizes limit certainty about long-term differences between progression strategies.

sources.title: Muscle Hypertrophy Is Affected by Volume Load Progression Models
sources.authors: Nóbrega SR, Scarpelli MC, Barcelos C, Chaves TS, Libardi CA
sources.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
sources.summaryEn: Exploratory secondary data analysis of 24 untrained men comparing a percentage-of-1RM progression model versus a repetition-zone (RM Zone) progression model, both performed to muscular failure over 24 training sessions. The RM Zone approach produced a significantly greater rate of volume-load progression (2.30 ± 0.58%/session vs. 1.01 ± 0.55%/session) and significantly greater muscle cross-sectional area gains than the %1RM approach, with no between-group difference in total accumulated volume load or 1RM strength gains. Small, exploratory secondary analysis in untrained men rather than a pre-registered primary trial; first author is Nóbrega SR, with Chaves TS as a co-author; epub was January 2022, print issue January 2023 (37(1):62-67).

sources.title: RPE vs. Percentage 1RM Loading in Periodized Programs Matched for Sets and Repetitions
sources.authors: Helms ER, Byrnes RK, Cooke DM, Haischer MH, Carzoli JP, Johnson TK, Cross MR, Cronin JB, Storey AG, Zourdos MC
sources.summaryEn: RCT in resistance-trained men (19-35y) comparing 8 weeks of daily-undulating squat/bench-press programming with loads assigned via percentage of 1RM (n=11) versus via RPE (participant-selected loads targeting an RPE range, n=10), matched for sets and repetitions. Both groups significantly increased bench press, squat, and combined-total 1RM, and pectoralis/vastus-lateralis muscle thickness, with no statistically significant between-group difference (p>0.05); magnitude-based inference indicated a 57-79% chance of a small strength advantage favoring RPE-based loading across lifts. Small sample size (n=21 total) and reliance on magnitude-based (not purely frequentist) inference limit certainty of the directional RPE advantage.

sources.title: Effects of subjective and objective autoregulation methods for intensity and volume on enhancing maximal strength during resistance-training interventions: a systematic review
sources.authors: Larsen S, Kristiansen E, van den Tillaar R
sources.summaryEn: Systematic review of 14 studies (30 training groups, 356 participants) comparing subjective (e.g., RPE/repetitions-in-reserve) and objective (e.g., velocity-based) autoregulation methods against non-autoregulated training for maximal-strength gains, requiring a comparison group and ≥4-week intervention for inclusion. All autoregulation protocols increased 1RM, with effect sizes ranging from small to large, suggesting autoregulation methods can be effective when embedded in a periodized plan. Heterogeneous study designs and autoregulation methods precluded a pooled quantitative meta-analysis.

sources.title: Effects of range of motion on resistance training adaptations: A systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.authors: Pallarés JG, Hernández-Belmonte A, Martínez-Cava A, Vetrovsky T, Steffl M, Courel-Ibáñez J
sources.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports
sources.summaryEn: PROSPERO-registered systematic review and meta-analysis (RoB 2 and GRADE-rated) of 16 studies comparing full versus partial range-of-motion resistance training on neuromuscular, functional, and structural adaptations. Full ROM training produced significantly greater gains in muscle strength (ES=0.56, p=0.004) and lower-limb hypertrophy (ES=0.88, p=0.027) than partial ROM, while functional performance favored full ROM non-significantly (ES=0.44, p=0.186) and no significant difference was found for muscle architecture (thickness, pennation angle, fascicle length; ES=0.28, p=0.226). Predates the more recent literature specifically isolating training at long muscle lengths ('lengthened partials'), so it does not distinguish that subtype from generic partial-ROM training.

sources.title: Optimizing Resistance Training Technique to Maximize Muscle Hypertrophy: A Narrative Review
sources.authors: Androulakis Korakakis P, Wolf M, Coleman M, Burke R, Piñero A, Nippard J, Schoenfeld BJ
sources.journal: Journal of Functional Morphology and Kinesiology
sources.summaryEn: Narrative review synthesizing evidence on resistance-training technique variables — exercise-specific kinematics, contraction type, repetition tempo, and range of motion — for maximizing muscle hypertrophy. Recommends training through a range of motion emphasizing long muscle lengths together with a repetition tempo of roughly 2-8 seconds, while explicitly noting that research on eccentric-versus-concentric phase manipulation and on universal kinematic guidelines remains limited. As a narrative review, its recommendations reflect the authors' synthesis of a still-developing evidence base rather than systematic or meta-analytic pooling.

sources.title: Greater Gastrocnemius Muscle Hypertrophy After Partial Range of Motion Training Performed at Long Muscle Lengths
sources.authors: Kassiano W, Costa B, Kunevaliki G, Soares D, Zacarias G, Manske I, Takaki Y, Ruggiero MF, Stavinski N, Francsuel J, Tricoli I, Carneiro MAS, Cyrino ES
sources.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
sources.summaryEn: RCT in 42 young women comparing 8 weeks of machine calf-raise training performed through full range of motion versus partial ROM confined to the initial (lengthened) or final (shortened) portion of ankle motion. Training in the initial/lengthened portion produced significantly greater medial gastrocnemius hypertrophy than full ROM or final-portion training (+15.2% vs +6.7% vs +3.4%, p≤0.009), and greater lateral gastrocnemius hypertrophy than final-portion training (+14.9% vs +6.2%, p<0.024), not significantly different from full ROM (+7.3%, p=0.060). Single-exercise, single-sex, 8-week study, so generalizability to other muscle groups, sexes, or longer durations is uncertain.

sources.title: Effects of squat training with different depths on lower limb muscle volumes
sources.authors: Kubo K, Ikebukuro T, Yata H
sources.summaryEn: RCT in 17 men comparing 10 weeks of full-depth versus half-depth back-squat training on lower-limb muscle volumes (MRI) and squat 1RM. Full-squat training produced significantly greater full-squat 1RM gains and significantly greater increases in adductor and gluteus maximus volume than half-squat training, while knee-extensor muscle volume increased similarly in both groups and rectus femoris/hamstring volumes did not change significantly in either group. Small single-exercise sample limits generalization to other lower-body movements.

sources.title: Greater Hamstrings Muscle Hypertrophy but Similar Damage Protection after Training at Long versus Short Muscle Lengths
sources.authors: Maeo S, Huang M, Wu Y, Sakurai H, Kusagawa Y, Sugiyama T, Kanehisa H, Isaka T
sources.summaryEn: Two-part within-subject controlled trial comparing seated (long muscle length) versus prone (short muscle length) leg-curl training in the same individuals over 12 weeks (n=20), plus a separate eccentric muscle-damage sub-study including 12 untrained controls. Seated (long-length) training produced significantly greater hamstring muscle-volume increases than prone (short-length) training (whole hamstrings +14% vs +9%), particularly in biarticular hamstring muscles, while monoarticular muscle gains did not differ; both trained conditions showed similarly much greater protection against exercise-induced muscle damage (T2 and strength-loss markers) than being untrained. Findings are specific to the leg-curl exercise and hamstrings; extrapolation to other muscle groups requires caution.

sources.title: What influence does resistance exercise order have on muscular strength gains and muscle hypertrophy? A systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.authors: Nunes JP, Grgic J, Cunha PM, Ribeiro AS, Schoenfeld BJ, de Salles BF, Cyrino ES
sources.summaryEn: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis (Hedges' g) of 11 good-to-excellent-quality studies (TESTEX-appraised, searched across four databases) examining resistance-exercise-order effects on strength and hypertrophy. Strength gains were largest for exercises performed earlier in the session: multi-joint-to-single-joint ordering favored multi-joint strength gains (ES=0.32, p=0.034), while single-joint-to-multi-joint ordering favored single-joint strength gains (ES=-0.58, p=0.032); across all exercises combined there was no overall order effect (ES=-0.11, p=0.306). Muscle hypertrophy showed no significant effect of exercise order (ES=0.03, p=0.862), with both sequencing strategies producing similar hypertrophy outcomes.

sources.title: No Time to Lift? Designing Time-Efficient Training Programs for Strength and Hypertrophy: A Narrative Review
sources.authors: Iversen VM, Norum M, Schoenfeld BJ, Fimland MS
sources.summaryEn: Narrative review evaluating how resistance-training variables and advanced techniques (supersets, drop sets, rest-pause training) affect time efficiency for strength and hypertrophy. Concludes such techniques can roughly halve session time while maintaining training volume and are likely more consistently effective for hypertrophy than for maximal strength, and recommends prioritizing multi-joint exercises and weekly set volume (a minimum of ~4 sets/muscle/week in a 6-15RM range) over training frequency. As a narrative review it synthesizes evidence qualitatively rather than through formal meta-analysis; the review drew published critical comments after release, and the authors themselves note more longitudinal research on these techniques is needed.

sources.title: American College of Sports Medicine position stand. Quantity and quality of exercise for developing and maintaining cardiorespiratory, musculoskeletal, and neuromotor fitness in apparently healthy adults: guidance for prescribing exercise
sources.authors: Garber CE, Blissmer B, Deschenes MR, Franklin BA, Lamonte MJ, Lee IM, Nieman DC, Swain DP; American College of Sports Medicine
sources.summaryEn: This ACSM position stand (superseding the 1998 ACSM position stand) recommends adults perform >=150 min/week moderate or >=75 min/week vigorous cardiorespiratory exercise, resistance exercise for major muscle groups on 2-3 days/week, plus flexibility and neuromotor (balance/agility/coordination) training. It states some exercise is better than none and that programs should be individualized to habitual activity, physical function, health status, and goals. As a synthesis position stand it does not report new primary experimental data.

sources.title: World Health Organization 2020 guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour
sources.authors: Bull FC, Al-Ansari SS, Biddle S, et al
sources.summaryEn: This WHO guideline update recommends adults perform 150-300 min/week moderate-intensity or 75-150 min/week vigorous-intensity aerobic activity, plus muscle-strengthening activity for all major muscle groups on >=2 days/week, and reduce sedentary time. It is based on systematic evidence reviews across age and population groups, adding new specific recommendations for pregnant/postpartum people and those with chronic conditions or disability, but the authors state evidence was insufficient to set a quantitative sedentary-behaviour threshold.

sources.title: Fundamentals of Resistance Training: Progression and Exercise Prescription
sources.authors: Kraemer WJ, Ratamess NA
sources.summaryEn: This narrative overview by two leading strength-training researchers describes the exercise-prescription process for progressive resistance training, covering needs analysis, exercise selection/order, rest intervals, and periodized progression of training variables to advance goals while avoiding overtraining. It is a conceptual/practical synthesis rather than a systematic review or primary study and does not itself report new experimental data.

sources.title: The Adaptations to Strength Training: Morphological and Neurological Contributions to Increased Strength
sources.authors: Folland JP, Williams AG
sources.summaryEn: This narrative review synthesizes evidence on morphological (whole-muscle and fiber cross-sectional area increases, satellite cell activation) and neurological (agonist activation, inter-muscular coordination, spinal reflexes) contributions to strength gains from resistance training. It concludes neurological factors likely make their greatest relative contribution early in training while hypertrophic processes also begin at training onset and increasingly dominate over time, noting some neurological evidence (e.g., on cortical/corticospinal excitability) is contradictory across studies.

sources.title: Early Resistance Training-Induced Increases in Muscle Cross-Sectional Area Are Concomitant with Edema-Induced Muscle Swelling
sources.authors: Damas F, Phillips SM, Lixandrao ME, Vechin FC, Libardi CA, Roschel H, Tricoli V, Ugrinowitsch C
sources.summaryEn: In this single-arm study of 10 untrained young men completing 10 weeks of resistance training, ultrasound-measured vastus lateralis cross-sectional area increased early (~2.7% by week 3) alongside elevated echo intensity and muscle-damage markers (myoglobin, IL-6), while measured strength (maximal voluntary contraction) increased only by week 10. The authors conclude early apparent size gains partly reflect edema-induced swelling from muscle damage rather than true hypertrophy; the small sample (n=10) and absence of a control group limit generalizability, and the authors themselves caution against labeling early CSA increases as pure hypertrophy.

sources.title: The Effect of Weekly Set Volume on Strength Gain: A Meta-Analysis
sources.authors: Ralston GW, Kilgore L, Wyatt FB, Baker JS
sources.summaryEn: This meta-analysis pooled 61 treatment groups from 9 studies (screened from 6962 records identified via PubMed, MEDLINE, SWETSWISE, EMBASE and SPORTDiscus as of September 2016) and found a graded dose-response relationship between weekly training sets and strength gains: high (HWS) and medium (MWS) weekly-set groups outperformed low weekly-set (LWS) groups for both multi-joint and isolation exercises (effect-size differences of roughly 0.15-0.23, all favoring higher volume). For well-trained individuals specifically, either MWS or HWS appears to be an appropriate dose, though the authors note their restrictive inclusion criteria left only 9 of 6962 screened studies eligible, limiting the precision of the dose-response estimate.

sources.title: The Minimum Effective Training Dose Required to Increase 1RM Strength in Resistance-Trained Men: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
sources.authors: Androulakis-Korakakis P, Fisher JP, Steele J
sources.summaryEn: This PRISMA/PROSPERO-registered (CRD42018108911) systematic review and meta-analysis screened 2629 studies and included 6 meeting inclusion criteria; a meta-analysis of 5 of those studies found that a single set of 6-12 reps at ~70-85% 1RM, performed 1-3 times/week for 8-12 weeks with high effort, was sufficient to produce significant though 'suboptimal' 1RM strength gains in resistance-trained men (pooled estimates: ~12.1kg overall, ~17.5kg squat, ~8.3kg bench press). The authors caution the evidence base is small (only 6-8 studies, single reviewer), that deadlift and trained-women/highly-trained-athlete data were insufficient to draw conclusions, and that results describe a minimum-effective (not optimal) training dose.

sources.title: Integrating Deloading into Strength and Physique Sports Training Programmes: An International Delphi Consensus Approach
sources.authors: Bell L, Strafford BW, Coleman M, Androulakis Korakakis P, Nolan D
sources.summaryEn: Using a 3-round Delphi process with 21-34 expert strength/physique coaches, this study built consensus design principles for integrating deload periods into training programs and proposed a definition of deloading as 'a period of reduced training stress designed to mitigate physiological and psychological fatigue, promote recovery, and enhance preparedness for subsequent training.' As an expert-consensus study it reflects practitioner opinion and experience rather than controlled experimental outcomes, so its principles are practice-based guidance pending direct experimental validation.

sources.title: Gaining More From Doing Less? The Effects of a One-Week Deload Period During Supervised Resistance Training on Muscular Adaptations
sources.authors: Coleman M, Burke R, Augustin F, Piñero A, Maldonado J, Fisher JP, Israetel M, Androulakis Korakakis P, Swinton P, Oberlin D, Schoenfeld BJ
sources.summaryEn: In this randomized controlled trial, 39 resistance-trained adults (29 men, 10 women) were assigned to a 9-week high-volume lower-body resistance training program either continuous (TRAD) or interrupted by a 1-week deload at the midpoint (DELOAD), with lower-body sessions supervised and upper-body sessions unsupervised (a noted limitation). Muscle-thickness, local-endurance, and power gains did not differ between groups, but TRAD showed greater improvements in lower-body isometric and dynamic strength and slightly better training-readiness scores than DELOAD, suggesting a single planned deload week may blunt strength gains without adding hypertrophy benefit in this population.

sources.title: Concurrent Training: A Meta-Analysis Examining Interference of Aerobic and Resistance Exercises
sources.authors: Wilson JM, Marin PJ, Rhea MR, Wilson SM, Loenneke JP, Anderson JC
sources.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
sources.summaryEn: This meta-analysis of 21 studies (422 effect sizes) found resistance training alone produced greater hypertrophy, strength, and power gains than endurance training alone, with concurrent training producing intermediate but still favorable effects versus endurance-only training. Interference on hypertrophy and strength was significant when the endurance component was running (but not cycling), and effect sizes correlated negatively with the frequency and duration of the endurance training, indicating the interference effect depends on the modality, frequency, and duration of the added endurance work.

sources.title: Compatibility of Concurrent Aerobic and Strength Training for Skeletal Muscle Size and Function: An Updated Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
sources.authors: Schumann M, Feuerbacher JF, Sünkeler M, Freitag N, Rønnestad BR, Doma K, Lundberg TR
sources.summaryEn: This PRISMA-guided, PROSPERO-registered (CRD42020203777) systematic review and meta-analysis of 43 studies found concurrent aerobic and strength training did not significantly compromise maximal strength (SMD -0.06, 95% CI -0.20 to 0.09, p=0.446) or muscle hypertrophy (SMD -0.01, 95% CI -0.16 to 0.18, p=0.919) versus strength training alone, but explosive strength gains were modestly attenuated (SMD -0.28, 95% CI -0.48 to -0.08, p=0.007), especially when aerobic and strength sessions were performed within the same session rather than separated by at least 3 hours. No significant moderating effects were found for aerobic modality (cycling vs running), training frequency, age, or training status.

sources.title: Development of Maximal Dynamic Strength During Concurrent Resistance and Endurance Training in Untrained, Moderately Trained, and Trained Individuals: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
sources.authors: Petré H, Hemmingsson E, Rosdahl H, Psilander N
sources.summaryEn: This systematic review and meta-analysis of 27 studies found concurrent resistance-and-endurance training negatively affected lower-body 1RM (leg press/squat) strength gains compared to resistance training alone in trained individuals (ES -0.35, p<0.01), but not in moderately trained (ES -0.20, p=0.08) or untrained individuals (ES 0.03, p=0.87). In trained individuals, the negative effect occurred specifically when endurance and resistance training were performed within the same session (ES -0.66, p<0.01) rather than in separate sessions (ES -0.10, p=0.55), indicating training status and same- vs different-session scheduling are key moderators of concurrent-training interference on strength.

sources.title: Effects of Strength Training on Running Economy in Highly Trained Runners: A Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis of Controlled Trials
sources.authors: Balsalobre-Fernández C, Santos-Concejero J, Grivas GV
sources.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
sources.summaryEn: This systematic review and meta-analysis of 5 controlled trials (93 competitive middle/long-distance runners) found strength-training programs (2-3x/week, 8-12 weeks, low-to-moderate loads plus plyometrics/sprints) produced a large improvement in running economy (SMD -1.42, 95% CI -2.23 to -0.60) versus non-strength-training controls. The evidence base was small (only 5 of 699 screened studies were eligible), limiting precision, though the authors judge the effect consistent enough to recommend strength training to improve running economy in highly trained runners.

sources.title: Effects of Strength Training on the Physiological Determinants of Middle- and Long-Distance Running Performance: A Systematic Review
sources.authors: Blagrove RC, Howatson G, Hayes PR
sources.summaryEn: This systematic review (24 studies, PEDro-assessed for methodological rigor, scores 4-6) found strength training generally improved running economy (2-8% in 20 studies), time-trial performance (1.5-10km), and anaerobic speed qualities in middle/long-distance runners without negatively affecting body composition, though improvements were not consistent across all included studies and VO2max/velocity at VO2max/lactate measures were typically unaffected. No meta-analysis was performed; the authors highlight methodological heterogeneity across studies as a limitation.

sources.title: Effects of Warming-up on Physical Performance: A Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis
sources.authors: Fradkin AJ, Zazryn TR, Smoliga JM
sources.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
sources.summaryEn: This systematic review and meta-analysis of 32 high-quality studies (quality score >6 on the Physiotherapy Evidence Database scale, mean 7.6/10) found warm-up activities improved subsequent physical performance in 79% of the outcomes examined, with little evidence that warming up harms performance. The authors note few well-conducted randomized controlled trials existed among the included literature, limiting causal certainty, and call for more RCTs to clarify warm-up's role in performance.

sources.title: Strength Testing—Predicting a One-Rep Max from Reps-to-Fatigue
sources.authors: Brzycki M
sources.journal: Journal of Physical Education, Recreation & Dance
sources.summaryEn: This practitioner-oriented paper describes a linear-approximation formula for estimating 1-repetition-maximum strength from a submaximal number of repetitions performed to fatigue, intended as a practical field-testing tool for coaches and teachers. This is a foundational/practice-oriented methods article rather than a data-driven validation study; no abstract text was retrievable via PubMed (not MEDLINE-indexed) or Semantic Scholar (abstract elided by publisher), so this summary is based on the verified title/scope only, and the formula's accuracy across exercises and rep ranges was subsequently tested by later validation studies (e.g., LeSuer et al. 1997).

sources.title: The Accuracy of Prediction Equations for Estimating 1-RM Performance in the Bench Press, Squat, and Deadlift
sources.authors: LeSuer DA, McCormick JH, Mayhew JL, Wasserstein RL, Arnold MD
sources.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
sources.summaryEn: This study by LeSuer, McCormick, Mayhew, Wasserstein, and Arnold compared several submaximal-repetition 1RM-prediction equations (e.g., Brzycki, Epley, and others) against actual measured 1RM values in trained lifters for bench press, squat, and deadlift. No abstract text was retrievable via PubMed (not indexed) or Semantic Scholar (abstract field elided by publisher), so this summary reports only the verified scope/purpose of the paper from its title and metadata; it is widely cited in later exercise-science literature as a key comparative validation of prediction-equation accuracy, but specific quantitative findings could not be independently confirmed here.

sources.title: The Epidemiology of Injuries Across the Weight-Training Sports
sources.authors: Keogh JWL, Winwood PW
sources.summaryEn: This systematic review of 20 eligible studies on injury epidemiology across weight-training sports (weightlifting, powerlifting, bodybuilding, strongman, Highland Games, CrossFit) found bodybuilding had the lowest injury rates (0.12-0.7 injuries/lifter/year) and strongman/Highland Games the highest (4.5-7.5 injuries/1000h), with shoulder, lower back, knee, elbow, and wrist/hand most commonly affected, and strains/tendinitis/sprains the most common injury types. Only 5 of 20 studies had a low risk-of-bias score and most used retrospective designs, so the authors call for more prospective, higher-quality epidemiological research.

sources.title: The Effectiveness of Exercise Interventions to Prevent Sports Injuries: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomised Controlled Trials
sources.authors: Lauersen JB, Bertelsen DM, Andersen LB
sources.summaryEn: This systematic review and meta-analysis of 25 RCTs (26,610 participants, 3,464 injuries) found strength training reduced sports-injury risk to less than one-third of control risk (RR 0.315, 95% CI 0.207-0.480) and roughly halved overuse injuries specifically (RR 0.527, 95% CI 0.373-0.746), while stretching showed no significant preventive effect (RR 0.963, 95% CI 0.846-1.095) and proprioception/multi-exposure programs showed intermediate benefit (RR 0.550 and 0.655 respectively). The authors note the overall pooled effect estimate was heterogeneous and a few outlying studies were present, though results for strength training specifically were consistently favorable.

sources.title: Inadequate sleep and muscle strength: Implications for resistance training
sources.authors: Knowles OE, Drinkwater EJ, Urwin CS, Lamon S, Aisbett B
sources.journal: Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport
sources.summaryEn: This systematic review of 17 studies (rated 'moderate' or 'weak' quality overall) examined effects of inadequate sleep on resistance-exercise performance, finding total sleep deprivation had little effect on muscle strength, but consecutive nights of sleep restriction could reduce force output in multi-joint (but not single-joint) movements. Hormonal responses to resistance training under inadequate sleep were conflicting across studies, and the authors suggest strategies like group training or caffeine to offset performance decrements, while cautioning that overall study quality limits certainty.

sources.title: Effect of range of motion in heavy load squatting on muscle and tendon adaptations
sources.authors: Bloomquist K, Langberg H, Karlsen S, Madsgaard S, Boesen M, Raastad T
sources.summaryEn: 12-week RCT in 17 male students randomized to deep squat (0-120° knee flexion, n=8) or shallow squat (0-60° knee flexion, n=9) training, repetition-matched with progressive RM-based loading. Deep-squat training produced superior increases in front-thigh muscle cross-sectional area (4-7%), isometric knee-extension strength (6-8% at 75° and 105°), and squat-jump performance (15%) versus shallow-squat training, with no group difference in patellar tendon CSA or collagen synthesis. Small, single-sex sample from one center; only two fixed ROM conditions were compared, not a full depth continuum.

sources.title: Full squat produces greater neuromuscular and functional adaptations and lower pain than partial squats after prolonged resistance training
sources.authors: Pallarés JG, Cava AM, Courel-Ibáñez J, González-Badillo JJ, Morán-Navarro R
sources.summaryEn: 10-week velocity-based RCT in 53 resistance-trained men randomized to four groups: full squat (F-SQ), parallel squat (P-SQ), half squat (H-SQ), and a training-cessation control, load-matched at 60-80% 1RM. F-SQ was the only group that increased 1RM and mean propulsive velocity at all three squat depths and achieved the highest functional-performance gains (countermovement jump, 20-m sprint, Wingate; ES 0.35-0.85), with P-SQ second best; H-SQ produced no significant neuromuscular or functional improvement and was the only group with significant increases in pain, stiffness and physical functional disability. Authors recommend F-SQ or P-SQ over H-SQ for strength and functional performance in well-trained athletes; outcomes are strength/velocity/functional/pain measures, not directly measured muscle hypertrophy, and the sample is limited to resistance-trained men.

sources.title: Hip thrust and back squat training elicit similar gluteus muscle hypertrophy and transfer similarly to the deadlift
sources.authors: Plotkin DL, Rodas MA, Vigotsky AD, McIntosh MC, Breeze E, Ubrik R, Robitzsch C, Agyin-Birikorang A, Mattingly ML, Michel JM, Kontos NJ, Lennon S, Frugé AD, Wilburn CM, Weimar WH, Bashir A, Beyers RJ, Henselmans M, Contreras BM, Roberts MD
sources.summaryEn: 9-week set-volume-equated RCT in untrained college-aged adults (hip thrust n=18, back squat n=16) with pre/post MRI muscle CSA and sEMG during the first session. Gluteal (lower/mid/upper) hypertrophy was similar between groups; squat produced greater quadriceps and adductor growth; each exercise produced the larger 3RM gain in its own trained lift, with similar deadlift and isometric wall-push strength transfer. Hip thrust elicited greater acute gluteal sEMG amplitude, but this did not consistently predict hypertrophy outcomes. Untrained sample, single center, 9-week duration.

sources.title: Back Squat vs. Hip Thrust Resistance-training Programs in Well-trained Women
sources.authors: Barbalho M, Coswig V, Souza D, Serrão JC, Hebling Campos M, Gentil P
sources.summaryEn: 12-week controlled trial in 22 well-trained women (back squat group n=12, hip thrust group n=10) measuring ultrasound muscle thickness and 1RM before/after. Back squat produced significantly greater quadriceps femoris (12.2% vs 2%, P<0.001) and gluteus maximus (9.4% vs 3.7%, P=0.001) thickness gains and greater back-squat 1RM increase (35.9% vs 4.3%, P<0.001) than hip thrust; hip-thrust 1RM improved similarly in both groups. Small single-sex sample (n=22); the abstract states participants were 'divided' into groups without explicitly stating a randomization method.

sources.title: A Comparison of Gluteus Maximus, Biceps Femoris, and Vastus Lateralis Electromyographic Activity in the Back Squat and Barbell Hip Thrust Exercises
sources.authors: Contreras B, Vigotsky AD, Schoenfeld BJ, Beardsley C, Cronin J
sources.summaryEn: Acute crossover EMG study in 13 trained women performing estimated 10RM back squat and barbell hip thrust. Hip thrust produced significantly greater mean and peak upper/lower gluteus maximus and biceps femoris EMG amplitude than back squat, with no difference in vastus lateralis activity. Authors explicitly note this acute activation difference does not establish that it translates into greater long-term strength or hypertrophy; longitudinal training studies were called for.

sources.title: The Impact of Back Squat and Leg-Press Exercises on Maximal Strength and Speed-Strength Parameters
sources.authors: Wirth K, Hartmann H, Sander A, Mickel C, Szilvas E, Keiner M
sources.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
sources.summaryEn: 8-week randomized controlled trial in 78 students (39 in training, split into squat and 45° leg-press subgroups; 39 matched controls) comparing the effects of parallel back squat vs. leg-press training on jump and strength outcomes. Squat training produced statistically significant gains in squat jump (12.4%) and countermovement jump (12.0%), while leg-press training produced smaller, non-significant gains (3.5% and 0.5% respectively); between-group differences favored the squat for jump-performance transfer, with indications it also improved drop-jump performance more effectively. Findings are specific to speed-strength/jump transfer in young non-elite trainees over a short intervention; hypertrophy was not assessed.

sources.title: Impact of exercise selection on hamstring muscle activation
sources.authors: Bourne MN, Williams MD, Opar DA, Al Najjar A, Kerr GK, Shield AJ
sources.summaryEn: Two-part observational study: surface EMG in 24 recreationally active men across 10 common hamstring exercises, followed by functional MRI in a subset comparing the exercises with the most and least selective biceps femoris (BF) activation. Eccentrically, the 45° hip-extension exercise produced the largest BF/medial-hamstring EMG ratio, while the Nordic hamstring exercise and bent-knee bridge had the lowest; concentrically, the lunge and 45° hip extension had the highest ratio and the leg curl and bent-knee bridge the lowest. fMRI showed a greater BF-long-head-to-semitendinosus activation ratio for the 45° hip extension than the Nordic exercise, and confirmed that the Nordic curl preferentially loads the semitendinosus. Acute activation/imaging data only; does not directly test chronic hypertrophy or injury-prevention outcomes from exercise selection.

sources.title: Regional Differences in Muscle Activation During Hamstrings Exercise
sources.authors: Schoenfeld BJ, Contreras B, Tiryaki-Sonmez G, Wilson JM, Kolber MJ, Peterson MD
sources.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
sources.summaryEn: Acute within-subject EMG study in 10 resistance-trained men comparing stiff-legged deadlift (hip-dominant) and lying leg curl (knee-dominant) performed to 8RM failure, with electrodes on upper/lower medial and lateral hamstrings. Lying leg curl produced significantly greater activation of the lower lateral and lower medial hamstrings than the stiff-legged deadlift, supporting the idea that exercise selection can regionally target the hamstrings. Acute EMG only; authors note it remains untested whether these activation differences produce regional hypertrophy differences over a training program.

sources.title: Including the Nordic hamstring exercise in injury prevention programmes halves the rate of hamstring injuries: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 8459 athletes
sources.authors: van Dyk N, Behan FP, Whiteley R
sources.summaryEn: Systematic review and meta-analysis pooling 15 studies (8459 athletes, multiple sports, both sexes) evaluating whether including the Nordic hamstring exercise (NHE) in injury-prevention programs reduces hamstring-injury incidence versus usual training or non-NHE programs. Pooled injury risk ratio was 0.49 (95% CI 0.32-0.74), with the protective effect remaining significant when restricted to the eight RCTs (RR 0.52) and after excluding high-risk-of-bias studies (RR 0.55), indicating roughly a 45-51% reduction. Included studies are heterogeneous in sport, program design, and injury-recording methods, and the analysis evaluates the NHE as part of broader programs rather than isolating its independent dose-response.

sources.title: Unilateral vs. Bilateral Squat Training for Strength, Sprints, and Agility in Academy Rugby Players
sources.authors: Speirs DE, Bennett MA, Finn CV, Turner AP
sources.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
sources.summaryEn: 5-week RCT in 18 academy rugby players randomized to unilateral rear-elevated split-squat training or bilateral back-squat training, twice weekly at matched relative intensity. Both groups showed significant, similar improvements in trained-lift 1RM, 40-m sprint time, and pro-agility performance, with no significant group-by-time interaction on any outcome, suggesting comparable short-term efficacy of unilateral and bilateral squat training. Short 5-week duration and single population (male academy rugby players); no muscle-hypertrophy outcome was measured.

sources.title: Specificity and Transfer of Lower-Body Strength: Influence of Bilateral or Unilateral Lower-Body Resistance Training
sources.authors: Appleby BB, Cormack SJ, Newton RU
sources.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
sources.summaryEn: 18-week randomized controlled training study in 33 developmental rugby players, with bilateral (back-squat, n=13), unilateral (step-up, n=10), and comparison (n=10) groups; an 8-week volume-load-matched training phase compared bilateral back-squat versus unilateral step-up resistance training. Both trained groups achieved practically important 1RM gains in their trained exercise, with partial transfer to the untrained exercise (bilateral group's step-up ES=0.27; unilateral group's squat ES=0.42). The unilateral group showed a clearer training-specific advantage in step-up strength (ES=0.41) than the between-group difference in squat-strength adaptation, which was unclear (ES=-0.34). Outcome measured is maximal-strength transfer only, not hypertrophy, in a single athletic (rugby) population.

sources.title: Triceps surae muscle hypertrophy is greater after standing versus seated calf-raise training
sources.authors: Kinoshita M, Maeo S, Kobayashi Y, Eihara Y, Ono M, Sato M, Sugiyama T, Kanehisa H, Isaka T
sources.summaryEn: 12-week within-subject training study in 14 untrained adults: one leg trained with standing/knee-extended calf raise (gastrocnemius lengthened) and the other with seated/knee-flexed calf raise (gastrocnemius shortened), matched load/volume, with pre/post MRI muscle-volume assessment. Standing calf raise produced substantially greater gastrocnemius hypertrophy than seated (lateral head +12.4% vs +1.7%; medial head +9.2% vs +0.6%), while soleus hypertrophy was similar between conditions (+2.1% vs +2.9%), consistent with a long-muscle-length training advantage specific to the biarticular gastrocnemius. Small sample of untrained adults and a single training protocol/machine.

sources.title: Analysis of the Load on the Knee Joint and Vertebral Column with Changes in Squatting Depth and Weight Load
sources.authors: Hartmann H, Wirth K, Klusemann M
sources.summaryEn: Non-systematic narrative literature review (over 164 articles, PubMed search March 2011-January 2013) synthesizing biomechanical and cadaveric evidence on knee-joint and spinal loading across squat depths. Concludes that concerns linking deep squats to greater degenerative knee/spine damage are largely unfounded given the 'wrapping effect' and enlarged patellar contact area at higher flexion, and that with proper technique and progressive loading deep squats are not inherently more injurious than half/quarter squats; the authors argue supra-maximal partial-squat loading may instead favor long-term degenerative change. As a narrative (non-systematic) review relying substantially on biomechanical modeling and cadaver studies rather than prospective injury-incidence cohorts, its safety conclusions are indirect.

sources.title: A three-dimensional biomechanical analysis of sumo and conventional style deadlifts
sources.authors: Escamilla RF, Francisco AC, Fleisig GS, Barrentine SW, Welch CM, Kayes AV, Speer KP, Andrews JR
sources.summaryEn: 3D kinematic/kinetic video analysis of 12 sumo-style and 12 conventional-style lifters filmed at a national powerlifting championship. Sumo deadlifts used a wider stance and more vertically oriented trunk/thighs and generated hip-extensor, knee-extensor, and ankle-dorsiflexor moments, whereas conventional deadlifts involved roughly 25-40% greater vertical bar travel, mechanical work, and predicted energy expenditure, plus additional knee-flexor and ankle-plantarflexor moments; ankle and knee moments/moment arms differed significantly between styles, but hip moments and moment arms did not. Observational competition-based analysis with no training intervention or hypertrophy/strength outcome; generalizes only to competitive powerlifters using their self-selected style.

sources.title: An electromyographic analysis of sumo and conventional style deadlifts
sources.authors: Escamilla RF, Francisco AC, Kayes AV, Speer KP, Moorman CT 3rd
sources.summaryEn: Acute EMG/video study in 13 collegiate football players performing sumo and conventional deadlifts at 12RM intensity, each with and without a lifting belt, recording 16 muscles across knee-angle intervals. Vastus medialis, vastus lateralis, and tibialis anterior activity were significantly greater in sumo deadlifts, medial gastrocnemius activity was greater in conventional deadlifts, and wearing a belt increased rectus abdominis activity while decreasing external oblique activity relative to no belt. Single-session acute EMG in trained male athletes; does not establish long-term strength, hypertrophy, or injury-risk effects of style or belt choice.

sources.title: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Common Therapeutic Exercises that Generate Highest Muscle Activity in the Gluteus Medius and Gluteus Minimus Segments
sources.authors: Moore D, Semciw AI, Pizzari T
sources.journal: International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy
sources.summaryEn: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 56 studies (from 6918 records screened across 7 databases) evaluating which common exercises generate at least high (>40% MVIC) surface EMG activity in gluteus medius (GMed) and gluteus minimus (GMin) segments. Hip hitch/pelvic-drop variations and standing isometric hip abduction reliably produced high activity across most GMed and GMin segments; single-leg bridge, side-lying hip abduction with internal rotation, lateral step-up, loaded standing hip abduction, and resisted side-step were the best options for the middle GMed segment specifically. Conclusions rest on acute surface-EMG amplitude across heterogeneous studies, not on measured strength gains or hypertrophy from training these exercises.

sources.title: Partial range of motion training elicits favorable improvements in muscular adaptations when carried out at long muscle lengths
sources.authors: Pedrosa GF, Lima FV, Schoenfeld BJ, Lacerda LT, Simões MG, Pereira MR, Diniz RCR, Chagas MH
sources.summaryEn: RCT in 45 untrained women randomized to full ROM, initial partial ROM (100-65° knee flexion, longer quadriceps length), final partial ROM (65-30°, shorter length), varied ROM (alternating initial/final), or non-training control in the knee-extension (leg extension) exercise, with regional quadriceps (rectus femoris and vastus lateralis) CSA at 40/50/60/70% of femur length and 1RM assessed pre/post. The initial (lengthened) partial-ROM group showed greater relative regional hypertrophy at several femur-length sites than full-ROM or final partial-ROM training; on 1RM, no group exceeded the varied-ROM or initial partial-ROM groups. Untrained women only, single exercise (leg extension), and regional CSA sampled at discrete femur-length percentages rather than whole-muscle volume.

sources.title: Large eccentric strength increase using the Copenhagen Adduction exercise in football: A randomized controlled trial
sources.authors: Ishøi L, Sørensen CN, Kaae NM, Jørgensen LB, Hölmich P, Serner A
sources.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports
sources.summaryEn: 8-week in-season RCT in 24 U-19 sub-elite football players (two teams randomized to intervention vs. control) evaluating a progressive Copenhagen Adduction (CA) exercise program added to usual training. Eccentric hip-adduction and hip-abduction strength were measured by a blinded tester at baseline and follow-up. The CA intervention group showed a significant 35.7% increase in eccentric hip-adduction strength (P<0.001) and a 20.3% increase in eccentric hip-abduction strength (P=0.003), with no significant change in controls; compliance was 91% with only mild-moderate soreness reported. Limitations: small sample of young sub-elite male footballers, short 8-week duration, team- (not individual-) level randomization, and strength (not hypertrophy or injury incidence) was the outcome measured.

sources.title: The Effects of Bench Press Variations in Competitive Athletes on Muscle Activity and Performance
sources.authors: Saeterbakken AH, Mo DA, Scott S, Andersen V
sources.summaryEn: In 12 national/international-level competitive bench press athletes, this acute EMG study compared 6RM competition-style (flat, wide-grip) bench press against narrow/medium grip widths and inclined/declined bench positions. Grip width and bench angle produced few significant EMG differences in the prime movers (pectoralis major, deltoids), but the inclined position markedly lowered triceps and raised biceps activity, and narrow grip reduced achievable 6RM load versus medium/wide grip. As a small, non-randomized acute study in trained athletes, findings describe activation patterns and 6RM strength, not hypertrophy outcomes, and may not generalize to untrained lifters.

sources.title: The Effect of Grip Width on Muscle Strength and Electromyographic Activity in Bench Press among Novice- and Resistance-Trained Men
sources.authors: Saeterbakken AH, Stien N, Pedersen H, Solstad TEJ, Cumming KT, Andersen V
sources.journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
sources.summaryEn: In 28 novice- and resistance-trained men, 6RM bench press with narrow, medium, and wide grips was compared via EMG. Biceps brachii activity rose and triceps brachii activity fell with wider grip, anterior deltoid activity was higher with medium versus narrow grip, and narrow grip reduced achievable 6RM load versus the other widths, with some differences between novice and trained subgroups. This is a single acute cross-sectional EMG/strength comparison, not a training study, so it cannot establish long-term hypertrophy or strength-gain differences between grip widths.

sources.title: The Influence of Grip Width and Forearm Pronation/Supination on Upper-Body Myoelectric Activity During the Flat Bench Press
sources.authors: Lehman GJ
sources.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
sources.summaryEn: This early EMG study measured isometric myoelectric activity of pectoralis major (sternoclavicular and clavicular portions), biceps brachii, and triceps brachii in 12 healthy men performing flat bench press across three grip widths and full supination/pronation. Supinated grip increased biceps and clavicular-pectoralis activity, and narrower grip increased triceps activity while decreasing sternoclavicular-pectoralis activity, though changes were described as small. The author explicitly cautions that, given the modest magnitude of changes, grip choice should be guided by sport specificity rather than attempts to isolate particular muscles; the isometric, single-session design does not address hypertrophy or injury outcomes.

sources.title: Effect of Five Bench Inclinations on the Electromyographic Activity of the Pectoralis Major, Anterior Deltoid, and Triceps Brachii during the Bench Press Exercise
sources.authors: Rodríguez-Ridao D, Antequera-Vique JA, Martín-Fuentes I, Muyor JM
sources.journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
sources.summaryEn: Thirty trained adults performed bench press at five bench angles (0°, 15°, 30°, 45°, 60°) at 60% 1RM while EMG of three pectoralis major regions, anterior deltoid, and triceps brachii was recorded. Upper-pectoralis activity peaked at the 30° incline, middle/lower pectoralis activity was highest at 0° (flat), anterior deltoid activity was highest at 60°, and triceps activity was similar across angles; inclines beyond 45° increased anterior deltoid activity while reducing pectoralis involvement. As an acute, single-session EMG study, it characterizes muscle activation patterns rather than long-term hypertrophic outcomes of different bench angles.

sources.title: Influence of Bench Angle on Upper Extremity Muscular Activation During Bench Press Exercise
sources.authors: Lauver JD, Cayot TE, Scheuermann BW
sources.summaryEn: Fourteen resistance-trained men performed one set of six barbell bench press repetitions at 0°, 30°, 45°, and -15° (decline) bench angles at 65% 1RM while surface EMG of upper and lower pectoralis major, anterior deltoid, and triceps brachii was recorded during both eccentric and concentric phases, each subdivided into four 25%-duration time points. Over the whole concentric phase, upper-pectoralis activation did not differ significantly across angles, but lower-pectoralis activation was significantly lower at 45° (71.9% MVIC) than at -15° (100.4%), 30° (86.6%), and horizontal (100.1%); time-point analysis also showed greater upper-pectoralis activity at 30° and 45° during 26-50% of the concentric contraction versus horizontal and decline. The authors conclude that a horizontal bench activates both the upper and lower pectoralis well, while incline angles of 30° or 45° increase activation at specific points in the range of motion; the small, single-session sample limits generalization to training-induced hypertrophy.

sources.title: Effects of Training With Free Weights Versus Machines on Muscle Mass, Strength, Free Testosterone, and Free Cortisol Levels
sources.authors: Schwanbeck SR, Cornish SM, Barss T, Chilibeck PD
sources.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
sources.summaryEn: In this 8-week randomized trial, 46 subjects (26 women, ~22 years old) trained major muscle groups with either free weights or machines (3-4 sets, 4-10 reps, 2-3x/week per muscle group). Biceps and quadriceps muscle thickness increased significantly in both groups with no between-group difference. On the machine bench press test, the machine-trained group gained more strength than the free-weight-trained group (13.9% vs 8.6%), while free-weight bench press and squat strength gains did not differ between groups. Men training with free weights showed a greater acute rise in free testosterone than men in the machine group, with no group difference in free cortisol response. The authors conclude free weights and machines produce broadly comparable hypertrophy and strength gains, with some strength adaptations specific to the trained modality; the short 8-week duration and modest sample limit long-term conclusions.

sources.title: Machines and free weight exercises: a systematic review and meta-analysis comparing changes in muscle size, strength, and power
sources.authors: Heidel KA, Novak ZJ, Dankel SJ
sources.journal: The Journal of Sports Medicine and Physical Fitness
sources.summaryEn: This systematic review and three-level random-effects meta-analysis (searches of PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science through September 2020) compared changes in muscle size, strength, and power between free-weight and machine-based resistance training. When strength was tested with a free-weight exercise, free-weight training produced greater gains (ES 0.655); when tested with a machine exercise, machine training produced greater gains (ES -0.784); when tested with a neutral device, gains were similar (ES 0.128), and no differences emerged for power (ES -0.049) or muscle hypertrophy (ES -0.01). The authors conclude that exercise choice for strength/power gains should be guided by test specificity, while for general strength and muscle mass, individuals may choose whichever modality they prefer and will adhere to.

sources.title: The Sticking Region in Three Chest-Press Exercises with Increasing Degrees of Freedom
sources.authors: Van den Tillaar R, Saeterbakken A
sources.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
sources.summaryEn: In 11 trained men, 1RM chest-press performance and EMG were compared across free barbell, Smith-machine, and dumbbell presses (increasing degrees of freedom). Free barbell allowed the highest 1RM load (106.4 kg), followed by Smith machine (103.6 kg), then dumbbells (89.5 kg); EMG activity and the length/timing of the sticking region differed between exercises but did not follow a simple pattern of increasing degrees of freedom producing a longer sticking region. The authors conclude exercise choice can bias particular muscles, but the small acute-testing sample (n=11) and single-repetition-maximum design limit inference about chronic hypertrophy or strength adaptations.

sources.title: Low-Load Bench Press and Push-Up Induce Similar Muscle Hypertrophy and Strength Gain
sources.authors: Kikuchi N, Nakazato K
sources.summaryEn: Eighteen young men were randomized to 8 weeks of either bench press or load-matched push-ups (~40% 1RM-equivalent load), twice weekly. Both groups significantly increased 1RM and triceps/pectoralis major muscle thickness with no between-group difference, though biceps thickness increased only in the bench-press group; neither power output nor muscular endurance changed in either group. The authors conclude push-ups at a matched relative load can produce hypertrophy and strength gains comparable to bench press for the trained muscles; sample size was small (n=9/group) and training duration short (8 weeks).

sources.title: Effects of Body Position and Loading Modality on Muscle Activity and Strength in Shoulder Presses
sources.authors: Saeterbakken AH, Fimland MS
sources.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
sources.summaryEn: Fifteen healthy men underwent EMG (at 80% 1RM load) and 1RM testing of barbell and dumbbell shoulder presses performed seated and standing. Standing with dumbbells (the least stable condition) produced the highest anterior, medial, and posterior deltoid EMG activity but the lowest 1RM load; barbell and seated conditions generally allowed greater load but somewhat lower deltoid activation. The authors conclude exercises with greater stability demands increase deltoid neuromuscular activity at the cost of load lifted; this acute single-session comparison in a modest sample does not directly measure training-induced hypertrophy or strength change.

sources.title: An Electromyographic Analysis of Lateral Raise Variations and Frontal Raise in Competitive Bodybuilders
sources.authors: Coratella G, Tornatore G, Longo S, Esposito F, Cè E
sources.journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
sources.summaryEn: Ten competitive bodybuilders performed lateral raise with externally, neutrally, and internally rotated humerus, a flexed-elbow lateral raise, and a frontal raise, with surface EMG recorded from anterior, medial, and posterior deltoid, pectoralis major, upper trapezius, and triceps brachii across concentric and eccentric phases. Internally rotated lateral raise produced the greatest posterior deltoid, triceps brachii, and upper-trapezius activation; the neutral-grip lateral raise produced the greatest medial deltoid activation among lateral-raise variants; and the frontal raise produced the greatest anterior deltoid and pectoralis major activation.
